MODULE 4 • TOPIC 1 • LESSON 2 537A


LESSON STRUCTURE AND PACING: 2 DAYS
DAY 1
ENGAGE
Getting Started: Are They Equal? 5 minutes
CONNECT TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE
Students determine whether expressions containing positive and negative exponents
are equivalent.

DEVELOP
Activity 2.1: Using Properties of Powers to Justify Steps in Simplifying 15–20 minutes
WORKED EXAMPLE, MATHEMATICAL PROBLEM SOLVING
Students are provided with expressions that have been rewritten using the properties of powers.
They examine the work and provide the mathematical justifications for each step. Students also
simplify expressions using the properties of powers and positive exponents.

Activity 2.2: Analyze Errors in Applying Properties of Powers 15–20 minutes
PEER WORK ANALYSIS
Students compare completed student work for simplifying two expressions using the properties
of powers. They determine the correct response and explain why the other responses are
not correct.

DAY 2
DEMONSTRATE
Talk the Talk: Organize the Properties 45 minutes
GRAPHIC ORGANIZER
Students create graphic organizers to organize their thoughts regarding the five properties
learned in this topic. The properties are the product of powers rule, the quotient of powers rule,
the power of a power rule, the zero power rule, and the negative exponent rule. For each rule,
they write a definition, list facts and characteristics, develop and solve example problems, and
then write a general rule for each property.

Getting Started
Compare and Contrast

ENGAGE

Facilitation Notes

In this activity, students review the fact that a geometric sequence has a
constant ratio between consecutive terms. They identify terms of a geometric
sequence given a recursive formula. Students then analyze graphs of geometric
sequences and are asked to identify similarities and differences among
the graphs.

Have students work with a partner or in a group to complete
Questions 1 through 3. Share responses as a class.
AS STUDENTS WORK, LOOK FOR
Confusion when to use the terms common ratio and constant ratio. Both
terms apply to the ratio when the interval between consecutive terms is
one; however, common ratio is used primarily for sequences, while constant
ratio is a more general term that may be applied to sequences, equations,
and functions. Remind students that they made the same adjustment with
common differences and constant differences, moving from arithmetic
sequences to linear functions.

may appear?

• Why are all the graphs discrete?
• Why aren’t any of the graphs lines?

The graphs of geometric sequences can be increasing, decreasing, or
alternating between increasing and decreasing.

In this activity, students revisit each graph of the geometric sequences from
the Getting Started, along with its corresponding equation and table of
values, and identify the constant ratio in each representation. They analyze
the graphs of the geometric sequences to realize that some geometric
sequences are exponential functions, while others are not.

Have students work with a partner or in a group to complete
Questions 1 through 3. Share responses as a class.

LESSON STRUCTURE AND PACING: 2 DAYS
DAY 1
ENGAGE
Getting Started: Match Game 15–20 minutes
CONNECT TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE
Students match four exponential functions to their graphs, connecting characteristics of
exponential graphs with the form of its corresponding equation. Students match exponential
functions to the scenarios the functions represent.

DEVELOP
Activity 2.1: Solving Exponential Equations by Graphing 20–25 minutes
REAL-WORLD PROBLEM SOLVING
Students model a depreciation scenario using an exponential function. They write a function
to represent the situation and then use it to construct a table of values and a graph. Students
estimate solutions by graphing constant functions on the coordinate plane and observing the
intersection point of each constant function with the exponential function.

DAY 2
Activity 2.2: Interpreting the B-value 25–30 minutes
PEER WORK ANALYSIS, WORKED EXAMPLE
Students explore a situation that shows the rate of increase of a mutual fund modeled by an
exponential function and then rewritten to show monthly and quarterly rates of increase.
Students use what they know about the constant ratio and exponent rules to rewrite equivalent
exponential functions that reveal different properties of the quantities represented.

DEMONSTRATE
Talk the Talk: Is This Uptown or Downtown? 10–15 minutes
EXIT TICKET APPLICATION
Students are presented with a scenario that gives the initial population of a city and the
population of the city five years later. They use what they know about the characteristics of
exponential functions that model growth and decay to identify appropriate exponential models
for the population of the city.
